newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi's capital boasts luxuries despite war.
newsitem.headline: Burundi's capital boasts luxuries despite war.

text.p: The countryside is violent and the people are fearful, but in the lakeside capital mobile phones and Belgian food help to hide the fact that Burundi is gripped in a ferocious civil war.
The yuppies around the hotel pool drink cold beer and chat into their phones while crested cranes peck at the nuts on the tables.
The "pop" of volleyed tennis balls is partially drowned as a truck passes with soldiers in camouflage fatigues and berets singing at the tops of their voices.
A short while later Burundi drummers dressed in the national flag's green, red and white pass by, beating out rhythms on the back of a speeding pick-up.
Hundreds attend mass in the Kirundi language in the Catholic cathedral, before heading for the market to buy something for Sunday lunch.

Sanctions -- imposed by surrounding African countries in protest at last July's military coup -- have hobbled the country, but vendors say trade in the city is normal. Salt is a bit more expensive than before and petrol is difficult to arrange, but flour is readily available and sales are brisk.

Up towards the hills which border the city to the east are large Mediterranean-inspired villas housing the moneyed classes and expatriates, along with the presidency occupied by Tutsi military ruler Pierre Buyoya.
Guards there stare at the passer-by, as do the gendarmes at the U.S. embassy where President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, a Hutu, has been since shortly before he was deposed in the July coup.

Some days the hills above ring with the sound of gunfire. The soldiers blame Hutu rebels. But they are in turn accused of trying to drive Hutu civilians into the countryside, as happened in Kamenge -- a desolate suburb overgrown and nearly deserted after Tutsi-led army operations against the residents.
Around 150,000 people -- mainly civilians -- have died in three years of fighting between rebels and the Tutsi-led army.

An officious soldier of indeterminate rank sits at a checkpoint between the vacant houses in Kamenge. The checkpoint has a chair in front of a table left when the owner fled, possibly to one of the Hutu refugee camps slightly up the hill.
There a family huddles under a piece of plastic, lucky to be around a pot that contains some beans from an aid agency.
Thousands of children play in the dirt outside, somehow managing to rustle up toothy grins despite the misery.

Across town near the sandy beaches of Lake Tanganyika are several dozen of the city's well-to-do, gathered at the yacht club under rakish palms for drinks and a chat after a few hours of messing around in their boats.
